domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on Nova Act computer-use agents—their architecture via act calls, RL-based exploration, and atomic interactions with UIs as a new agent paradigm. The talk covers general-purpose computer-use agents without tying to a specific application vertical. Nova Act is explicitly described as a research preview with model improvements shipped every few weeks. Demos are accessible but the cognitive science framing and agent architecture discussion require technical familiarity. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. All supporting evidence is directly quoted from the transcript with said_in_transcript grade.

summary: Danielle Perszyk, cognitive scientist at Amazon's AGI SF Lab, frames her talk around the reliability of human intelligence. Neuroscientists describe brains as prediction machines and perception as controlled hallucination—hallucinations are features enabling flexibility, not bugs, but control is critical. She distinguishes two historical perspectives: the 1956 Dartmouth goal of building thinking machines (AGI) versus Douglas Engelbart's vision of augmenting human intelligence via tools like the mouse and GUI. She introduces technosocial co-evolution: technologies we invent shape us in return. Automation doesn't always augment—scrolling, echo chambers, and autocomplete can reduce agency. The lab's vision is to build AI that increases human agency, "unhobbling humans." Nova Act is their research preview: a UI-specialized Amazon Nova model with an SDK. An "act call" translates natural language to screen actions. Demos include apartment search in Redwood City, structured extraction with Pydantic, parallel browser workflows with thread pools, and pandas tabulation—all in roughly three lines of code, with model updates every few weeks. Computer-use basics are deceptively hard, requiring RL for exploration. Computer-use agents see pixels, interact with UIs, and have early embodiment, unlike LLM wrappers lacking world models. Nova Act focuses on reliable atomic interactions with granular control. She then traces intelligence's evolution back six million years: ancestors solved intelligence through a feedback loop where bigger brains enabled social connection, which further enlarged brains. Humans offloaded computation across social environments via representational alignment. Language co-evolved with models of minds in a flywheel where models of mind became the first placeholder concept for representing any concept—that is generalization. Unlike programming languages, human language negotiates meaning in real time; LLMs don't understand that words refer to things minds make up. Language triggered cognitive technologies—tools for thought that stabilize thinking and control hallucinations by directing attention to shared environmental signals. Nova Act is framed as primitives for a cognitive technology aligning agent and human representations. Agents can become our collective subconscious, doing repetitive work, redistributing skills, and teaching new knowledge. Reliability requires understanding goals, which eventually needs agents with models of our minds. These must emerge from preconditions: a shared environment model, intuitive interfaces, human-agent interaction data, and useful products. The more useful the products, the smarter we all become.

sections.title: Cognitive Science Framing: Controlled Hallucination and General Intelligence
sections.summary: Danielle introduces herself as a cognitive scientist at Amazon AGI SF Lab. She frames human brains as prediction machines engaged in controlled hallucination—hallucinations are necessary features enabling flexible intelligence, but control is the critical part. She argues we need AI that complements rather than replicates humans, and that AGI as 'intelligence within a thinking machine' reflects a category error about how intelligence actually works.

sections.title: Historical Perspectives: Thinking Machines vs. Augmenting Humans
sections.summary: She contrasts two lineages: the 1956 founding of AI aimed at building thinking machines, versus Douglas Engelbart's vision of augmenting human intelligence through tools like the mouse and GUI. She introduces technosocial co-evolution—the idea that technologies we invent shape us—and argues that automation doesn't always augment; it can reduce agency through scrolling, echo chambers, and autocomplete. The lab's vision is to build AI that increases human agency.

sections.title: Nova Act: Vision, SDK, and Demonstrations
sections.summary: She introduces Nova Act as a research preview combining a UI-specialized Amazon Nova model with an SDK. The atomic unit is an 'act call' translating natural language to screen actions. Demos show apartment search in Redwood City, structured extraction with Pydantic, Google Maps biking distance to CalTrain, parallel browsers via thread pool, and pandas tabulation—all in ~3 lines of code, with model updates every few weeks.

sections.title: Computer-Use Challenges, RL, and Agent Evolution
sections.summary: She explains that computer-use basics are deceptively hard (e.g., interpreting unlabeled icons), requiring RL for exploration. She contrasts computer-use agents—which see pixels, interact with UIs, and have early embodiment—with LLM-wrapper assistants lacking world models. Nova Act focuses on reliable atomic interactions with granular control. She concludes that shared environmental grounding is necessary but not sufficient for aligned general-purpose agents, setting up further discussion of how Nova Act must evolve.

sections.title: Evolutionary Origins and Language as Cognitive Technology
sections.summary: She traces intelligence's evolution back six million years: ancestors solved intelligence through a feedback loop where bigger brains enabled social connection, which further enlarged brains. Humans offloaded computation across social environments via representational alignment. Language co-evolved with models of minds in a flywheel where models of mind became the first placeholder concept for representing any concept—that is generalization. Unlike programming languages, human language negotiates meaning in real time; LLMs don't understand that words refer to things minds make up. General intelligence is social, distributed, and emerges through interactions, not in individual models.

sections.title: Agents as Collective Subconscious and the Path to Useful General Intelligence
sections.summary: Language triggered cognitive technologies—tools for thought that stabilize thinking and control hallucinations by directing shared attention to environmental signals. Nova Act is framed as primitives for a cognitive technology aligning agent and human representations, needing to evolve in diverse communities. Agents can become our collective subconscious, doing repetitive work, redistributing skills, and teaching new knowledge. Reliability requires understanding goals, which eventually needs agents with models of our minds. These emerge from preconditions: a shared environment model, intuitive interfaces, human-agent interaction data, and useful products that motivate adoption, enabling reciprocal leveling of intelligence.
